items.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm packages Kubernetes applications as charts, which are directories of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax.
The `helm` CLI either installs rendered chart manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories.
Helm charts are indexed publicly on Artifact Hub (artifacthub.io).
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm project does not ship a commercial tier or managed service.
Pulumi programs can be authored in general-purpose languages with loops, conditionals, classes, and package management.
Pulumi supports YAML as an authoring language for infrastructure programs.
Pulumi supports HCL as an authoring language for infrastructure programs.
Helm charts are authored as YAML manifests with Go template syntax and take inputs through a `values.yaml` file.
Pulumi derives resource ordering from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready before it is created.
Pulumi deploys independent resources (resources with no dependency relationship) in parallel.
Helm applies the resources in a release in a fixed order determined by Kubernetes kind, implemented in the Helm source file `pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go`.
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between individual resources or between subcharts to control install ordering (negative capability claim — verify against Helm docs/source).
Helm chart hooks can be ordered using `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations (hook weights), which is the only Helm-native mechanism for ordering within a release.
Pulumi Automation API is a programmatic SDK available in every Pulumi-supported language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Policies (Pulumi's policy-as-code framework) is open source.
Pulumi Policies supports writing policy rules in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management on top of Pulumi Policies.
The Pulumi Cloud Enterprise edition includes Pulumi-maintained pre-built policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy-as-code engine.
With Helm, policy enforcement is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
Pulumi (the pulumi/pulumi project) is open source under the Apache License 2.0.

The Helm docs (Charts → Operational aspects of using dependencies) state: "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."
Helm's kind-sort order begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC objects, then Services and workloads.
In Helm's install order, any Kubernetes kind not on the hardcoded kind-sort list (including custom resources) is applied last.
Helm uninstall deletes resources using the same kind-sort list in reverse order.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the Kubernetes API server in a single pass and does not wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.

Per the Helm docs, a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's object set and sorted by kind along with everything else, so chart dependencies do not affect install ordering (declaring a subchart as a dependency does not make it install first).
Resources created by Helm chart hooks are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
HIP-0025 (helm.sh/community/hips/hip-0025) proposes native sequencing for resources and subcharts in Helm.
HIP-0025 is still in draft status (not accepted or implemented).
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output as an input to another resource creates an edge in the dependency graph.
Setting the `dependsOn` resource option in Pulumi creates an explicit edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each Kubernetes resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it.
Pulumi updates are faster than a strict serial sequence because independent resources are deployed in parallel.
Pulumi deletes resources following the dependency graph in reverse order.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider's `helm.v4.Chart` resource supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart.
`dependsOn` set on a `helm.v4.Chart` resource expresses dependencies on Pulumi resources outside the chart.
Helm manages Kubernetes resources only; resources outside the cluster (managed databases, DNS records, IAM roles, managed Redis) require another tool.
A Helm chart can install Custom Resource Definitions, workloads, services, and other manifests into a cluster.
Pulumi can manage non-Kubernetes cloud/SaaS resources and Kubernetes resources together in one program via the Pulumi Registry.
The Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms including Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm records each install or upgrade of a release as a numbered release revision.
`helm rollback` restores a release to a prior revision from its release history.
Pulumi can run through the local CLI, programmatically through the Automation API, or remotely through Pulumi Deployments.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack in a partially updated state; recovery is roll-forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release, whereas Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns (end-to-end cluster orchestration and wiring Pulumi outputs into chart values) cover most production deployments of Pulumi with Helm.

A single Pulumi program can create a Kubernetes cluster (EKS, AKS, or GKE), configure networking and IAM, and install Helm charts such as cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/eks/ exists and walks through creating a cluster and installing the operational stack end-to-end.

The Pulumi Helm chart resources' `values` input accepts the same shape as a `values.yaml` file, and each leaf value can be a typed Pulumi output from another resource (e.g. an `aws.rds.Instance` connection string, a KMS key ARN, a Cloudflare zone ID).
Pulumi resolves output values passed into a Helm chart's `values` at deploy time and orders the chart install after the resources those outputs come from.
The in-page anchors #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease, #resource-ordering-and-dependencies, and #adoption-coexistence-conversion-and-import exist on this page.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm (use charts directly, convert charts, import resources), and they can be combined.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program and migrating incrementally is the most common Pulumi adoption pattern for Helm users.
`pulumi convert --from kubernetes` converts Kubernetes YAML (such as output of `helm template`) into native Pulumi code.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option bring existing in-cluster Kubernetes resources under Pulumi management and generate the corresponding program code.
The guide "Migrating from Kubernetes YAML or Helm Charts to Pulumi" exists at /docs/iac/guides/migration/migrating-to-pulumi/from-kubernetes/.
A Pulumi program can pull Helm charts from any Helm repository, public or private.

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child appears in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster.
`helm.v3.Release` preserves Helm-specific behaviors including chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.
Pulumi recommends choosing `helm.v4.Chart` for fine-grained visibility into every rendered resource and `helm.v3.Release` when the chart relies on hooks or other Helm-specific lifecycle behavior.
Pulumi can replace Helm, but does not have to; teams can keep installing upstream charts from Pulumi or convert charts to native Pulumi code.
